overview: For four centuries one government ruled every shore of the Mediterranean, from the Atlantic to the Euphrates and from Hadrian's Wall to the first cataract of the Nile. Rome invented little that was wholly new and perfected almost everything it borrowed: Greek architecture became concrete vaults, Etruscan drains became aqueducts, and a city-state's customs became a body of law that most of Europe still lives under. Its language, Latin, is the parent of Spanish, Portuguese, French, Italian and Romanian.

items.text: Roman concrete, opus caementicium, mixed with volcanic ash so that it set even under water. The harbour moles built with it at Caesarea and Portus still stand.
Vitruvius completes De architectura, ten books on building, water, machines and city planning that guided Renaissance architects fifteen centuries later.
The Colosseum opens: about 50,000 seats, a retractable awning, and eighty entrances so the whole crowd could leave in minutes.
The Pantheon's concrete dome, 43.3 meters across, is completed under Hadrian. It is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world.
Pliny the Elder publishes the Natural History, thirty-seven books that try to gather everything then known about the natural world.
Ptolemy, working in Alexandria, writes the Almagest, the geocentric model of the heavens that stood for 1,400 years, and a Geography that placed the known world on a grid of coordinates.
Galen arrives in Rome. His dissections of animals describe the nerves, the heart and the pulse, and his anatomy is taught in Europe until the sixteenth century.
Aqueducts: eleven serve the city of Rome by 226 CE, feeding public fountains, baths and a sewer system, the Cloaca Maxima, that still drains the Forum.
Roads: about 80,000 km of paved highway across the empire by the second century, cambered for drainage, with milestones and way stations a day's ride apart.
The codex, pages bound at the spine, begins to replace the scroll; by the fourth century it is the normal form of the book.
The mills at Barbegal near Arles: sixteen water wheels in two descending rows, grinding grain for a whole town.
Virgil dies leaving the Aeneid unfinished. Augustus orders it published against the poet's wishes, and it becomes Rome's national epic.
Ovid completes the Metamorphoses, the retelling of Greek and Roman myth that fed European painting and poetry for two thousand years.
Trajan's Column: a 30-meter spiral of carved relief telling the story of the Dacian wars in 155 scenes.
Portrait sculpture that shows the sitter warts and all, mosaic floors from Britain to Syria, and the wall paintings of Pompeii, sealed by Vesuvius in 79 CE.
Roman law: the praetors' edicts and the jurists' commentaries, later gathered under Justinian, are the root of the civil law systems of continental Europe and Latin America.
Seneca, Stoic philosopher and tutor to Nero, is ordered to kill himself, leaving the Letters to Lucilius. Stoicism was the working philosophy of the Roman elite.
Constantine's Edict of Milan grants freedom of worship. Christianity, persecuted a decade earlier, becomes the religion of the emperors.
The Edict of Thessalonica makes Nicene Christianity the state religion.
Public baths in every town, with hot and cold rooms, exercise yards and libraries. Entry cost a quadrans, the smallest coin.

A market the size of the Mediterranean: Spanish olive oil, Egyptian grain, Gaulish wine and Indian pepper moved in amphorae. Monte Testaccio in Rome is a hill made of an estimated 53 million broken oil jars.
Insulae, apartment blocks of five or more storeys, housed most of Rome's roughly one million people, the largest city in the world until the nineteenth century.

fall.text: On the death of Theodosius I in 395 the empire was divided between his sons Arcadius and Honorius and never reunited. The Western half fell in 476; the Eastern half, which we call Byzantine, lasted until 1453.

sources.title: Mary Beard, SPQR: A History of Ancient Rome (2015)
